difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that algorithmic content curation shapes user behavior; the disagreement turns on a presupposition — whether this shaping constitutes manipulation requiring regulation — which is buried beneath overlapping common ground. Three distractors reflect genuine points of partial agreement, and identifying the precise axis of disagreement requires close reading.
stimulus: Moreno: Algorithmic content curation inevitably shapes what users believe and value. Because this influence is exercised without users' informed consent, platforms that deploy such algorithms should be subject to regulatory oversight. The power to shape belief at scale is simply too significant to leave unexamined. Peña: I agree that algorithms influence user behavior, and that this influence can be profound. But shaping behavior is not the same as manipulation. Every environment — a bookstore, a classroom — shapes what people are exposed to. Imposing regulatory oversight on content curation would therefore threaten the editorial freedom that makes diverse platforms possible.
questionStem: Moreno and Peña's statements provide the most support for the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: algorithmic content curation has any influence on user beliefs and values

choices.label: B
choices.text: bookstores and classrooms shape what people are exposed to

choices.label: C
choices.text: platforms' use of content-curation algorithms warrants regulatory oversight

choices.label: D
choices.text: the influence of content-curation algorithms can be profound

choices.label: E
choices.text: users are aware of the extent to which algorithms shape their beliefs

explanations.correct: Moreno explicitly concludes that platforms using content-curation algorithms should be subject to regulatory oversight; Peña explicitly concludes that imposing such oversight would threaten editorial freedom — meaning Peña opposes it. Both take clear, opposed positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: This is a point of agreement. Peña concedes in the second sentence that 'algorithms influence user behavior' and 'this influence can be profound.' Neither speaker denies the influence exists.
explanations.B: Peña asserts this as an analogy; Moreno never addresses it. This is a one-sided trap — only one speaker takes a position.
explanations.C: Correct. Moreno affirms oversight is warranted; Peña denies it, arguing oversight would threaten editorial freedom.
explanations.D: Another point of agreement — Peña explicitly concedes the influence 'can be profound,' and Moreno's argument presupposes it. No disagreement here.
explanations.E: Moreno mentions lack of informed consent, which implies limited user awareness, but Peña never addresses user awareness at all. One-sided trap.

difficultyReason: Both speakers value biodiversity and agree that invasive species cause harm; their disagreement is about degree — specifically whether eradication programs are justified when they also damage native ecosystems. The correct answer is a conditional proposition that requires inferring each speaker's implicit commitment, while three distractors exploit the shared common ground.
stimulus: Dr. Chen: Invasive species eradication programs are justified even when the removal methods — pesticides, trapping, controlled burns — cause collateral damage to native ecosystems. The long-term benefit of restoring ecological balance outweighs short-term harm to native species. Biodiversity ultimately recovers more fully without the invasive pressure. Dr. Okonkwo: Eradication programs can be valuable, but only when removal methods do not themselves significantly degrade the native ecosystem. Causing serious harm to native species in order to eliminate an invasive one trades one ecological injury for another. The goal of protecting biodiversity cannot justify methods that undermine it.
questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Invasive species exert harmful pressure on native ecosystems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biodiversity is a goal worth protecting through conservation programs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An eradication program that causes significant collateral damage to native species can nonetheless be justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eradication programs are never an appropriate conservation tool.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Controlled burns are more damaging to native ecosystems than pesticide use.

explanations.correct: Dr. Chen explicitly affirms that eradication is justified even when removal methods cause collateral damage to native ecosystems. Dr. Okonkwo explicitly denies this, arguing that methods causing serious harm to native species are not justified regardless of intent. Both take clear, opposed positions.
explanations.A: Both speakers accept this. Dr. Chen's argument presupposes invasive species harm native ecosystems, and Dr. Okonkwo never contests it. Agreement in disguise.
explanations.B: Both speakers take biodiversity protection as a shared goal — Dr. Chen argues eradication ultimately serves it; Dr. Okonkwo argues methods must not undermine it. Agreement in disguise.
explanations.D: Dr. Okonkwo explicitly says eradication 'can be valuable,' so both speakers agree eradication is sometimes appropriate. Agreement in disguise; also a shift in subject from 'when justified' to 'ever justified.'
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses the relative harm of different removal methods. Out-of-scope trap.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree historical atrocities should be acknowledged; the disagreement is about whether acknowledgment requires institutional reparations or is fulfilled by other means. The correct answer requires identifying that one speaker treats acknowledgment and reparations as separable while the other treats them as linked, a nuanced presuppositional disagreement. Two distractors represent agreements; one is one-sided.
stimulus: Lourdes: Nations that have committed historical atrocities against identifiable communities owe those communities material reparations. Acknowledging wrongdoing through memorials and apologies is important, but acknowledgment alone does not repair the economic and social harm that persists to the present day. Only material redress fulfills the full moral obligation. Tariq: Historical acknowledgment — formal apologies, educational curricula, public memorials — is a genuine and complete form of moral redress. Demanding material reparations conflates two distinct obligations: the duty to remember and the duty to compensate. Nations bear the first duty clearly; whether they bear the second is far less certain.
questionStem: Lourdes and Tariq disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: nations that committed historical atrocities have an obligation to acknowledge the wrongdoing

choices.label: B
choices.text: public memorials and formal apologies constitute meaningful acts of redress

choices.label: C
choices.text: the economic and social harm caused by historical atrocities can persist into the present day

choices.label: D
choices.text: a nation's moral obligations regarding historical atrocities are fully discharged by acknowledgment alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: the duty to remember past atrocities is a genuine moral obligation

explanations.correct: Lourdes explicitly denies that acknowledgment alone fulfills the full moral obligation, insisting material reparations are also required. Tariq explicitly affirms that acknowledgment is 'a genuine and complete form of moral redress.' Both take opposed positions on whether acknowledgment alone is sufficient.
explanations.A: Both agree on this. Lourdes calls acknowledgment 'important'; Tariq calls it 'a genuine and complete form.' Agreement in disguise.
explanations.B: Lourdes implicitly accepts that memorials and apologies are meaningful (calling them 'important'); Tariq affirms this explicitly. Both agree — agreement in disguise.
explanations.C: Lourdes asserts this; Tariq never disputes it, focusing instead on whether material redress follows from it. One-sided trap.
explanations.E: Both accept this — Lourdes presupposes it; Tariq explicitly states nations 'bear the first duty clearly.' Agreement in disguise.

difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that central bank independence has costs; the correct disagreement is about whether those costs are outweighed by the benefits of insulating monetary policy from electoral cycles — a comparative-weight judgment requiring inference from each speaker's reasoning rather than explicit statement. Multiple distractors involve points where both speakers' positions converge.
stimulus: Vasquez: Central banks should be insulated from electoral politics. When monetary policy is subject to short-term political pressure, governments inflate currency to win elections, producing long-run instability. The loss of democratic accountability is a real cost, but it is outweighed by the macroeconomic stability that independence provides. Ingrid: Democratic accountability is not merely a cost to be weighed against economic efficiency — it is a foundational requirement of legitimate governance. A central bank that operates beyond meaningful public oversight, however technically proficient, undermines the principle that consequential collective decisions must ultimately answer to the public. The stability argument, though not without merit, does not override this.
questionStem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Vasquez and Ingrid disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: politically influenced monetary policy can produce long-run economic instability

choices.label: B
choices.text: central bank independence involves any reduction in democratic accountability

choices.label: C
choices.text: democratic accountability is a value that carries some weight in evaluating monetary policy institutions

choices.label: D
choices.text: macroeconomic stability is a legitimate consideration in designing monetary policy institutions

choices.label: E
choices.text: the macroeconomic benefits of central bank independence outweigh the reduction in democratic accountability it entails

explanations.correct: Vasquez explicitly concludes that the loss of democratic accountability 'is outweighed by macroeconomic stability.' Ingrid explicitly states that 'the stability argument does not override' the democratic-accountability requirement. Both take directly opposed positions on the weight comparison.
explanations.A: Vasquez asserts this; Ingrid calls the stability argument 'not without merit,' implying she accepts it as at least partially valid. Neither denies it — this is a point of agreement or at most a one-sided point.
explanations.B: Both speakers accept this. Vasquez calls it 'a real cost'; Ingrid treats it as a foundational concern. Agreement in disguise.
explanations.C: Both accept democratic accountability carries weight. Vasquez weighs it against stability; Ingrid treats it as foundational. Agreement — the disagreement is about how much weight, not whether it has any.
explanations.D: Ingrid calls the stability argument 'not without merit,' and Vasquez affirms it. Both accept macroeconomic stability as a legitimate consideration. Agreement in disguise.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that eyewitness testimony is sometimes unreliable; the precise disagreement is about whether its unreliability is sufficiently systematic to warrant a categorical legal rule excluding it absent corroboration — a conditional proposition. The correct answer is harder to identify because both speakers engage similar evidence but draw opposite structural conclusions. Two distractors capture genuine agreements; one is a near-miss that shifts the subject.
stimulus: Holloway: Eyewitness testimony should not be admitted as the sole basis for a criminal conviction. Decades of cognitive research demonstrate that memory is reconstructive, not reproductive — eyewitnesses frequently misidentify strangers, and confidence does not correlate with accuracy. Given the stakes, no conviction should rest on uncorroborated eyewitness identification alone. Soren: Eyewitness testimony is fallible, as the research confirms. But fallibility is not grounds for categorical exclusion. Cross-examination, jury instructions, and expert witnesses allow juries to weigh eyewitness evidence appropriately. Excluding uncorroborated testimony as a matter of rule would override that judgment and discard probative evidence in many cases where it is in fact reliable.
questionStem: Holloway and Soren's statements provide the most support for the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: eyewitness testimony is sometimes unreliable

choices.label: B
choices.text: a witness's level of confidence in an identification is a reliable indicator of that identification's accuracy

choices.label: C
choices.text: cross-examination is a procedure available to defendants in criminal trials

choices.label: D
choices.text: uncorroborated eyewitness testimony should be categorically excluded as the sole basis for a criminal conviction

choices.label: E
choices.text: cognitive research on memory has produced findings relevant to evaluating eyewitness testimony

explanations.correct: Holloway explicitly argues that no conviction should rest on uncorroborated eyewitness identification alone — a categorical rule of exclusion. Soren explicitly argues against such categorical exclusion, contending that existing trial procedures suffice. Both take directly opposed positions on this proposition.
explanations.A: Both agree eyewitness testimony is sometimes unreliable. Holloway relies on this; Soren concedes it ('fallible, as the research confirms'). Agreement in disguise.
explanations.B: Holloway asserts confidence does not correlate with accuracy; Soren never addresses this claim. One-sided trap — only one speaker takes a position.
explanations.C: Neither speaker disputes that cross-examination exists; Soren invokes it as a safeguard. Holloway does not deny it. Out-of-scope or at most one-sided.
explanations.E: Both accept cognitive research as relevant. Holloway relies on it; Soren concedes it ('the research confirms'). Agreement in disguise.

difficultyReason: Both speakers affirm that literary fiction can convey truth; the disagreement is about whether fiction's value depends primarily on that truth-conveying function or is instead grounded in aesthetic experience independent of any epistemic payoff. The correct answer requires the reader to infer each speaker's implicit position on the relationship between aesthetic and epistemic value — neither states it with full explicitness. Three distractors are plausible near-misses.
stimulus: Renata: The enduring value of literary fiction lies in its capacity to illuminate truths about human experience that discursive prose cannot reach. A novel can render the texture of grief or the logic of moral failure more precisely than any philosophical treatise. Fiction earns its place in the curriculum because of what it teaches us about how to live. Dmitri: Fiction can certainly illuminate aspects of human experience, and I do not dismiss that function. But reducing fiction's value to its epistemic yield misses what is most irreplaceable about it: the aesthetic encounter itself — rhythm, structure, surprise — which has worth independently of any lesson imparted. A novel is not primarily a vehicle for truth; it is a made object whose form is its own justification.
questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Renata and Dmitri are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Literary fiction can illuminate truths about human experience that are difficult to convey through discursive prose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The aesthetic properties of a literary work — its rhythm, structure, and form — have some value.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The primary source of literary fiction's value is its capacity to convey truths about human experience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Literary fiction has any place in an educational curriculum.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Philosophical treatises are less effective than fiction at conveying moral insight.

explanations.correct: Renata explicitly argues fiction's value lies in illuminating truths — 'what it teaches us about how to live' — making its epistemic yield primary. Dmitri explicitly argues that 'reducing fiction's value to its epistemic yield misses what is most irreplaceable' and that the aesthetic encounter 'has worth independently of any lesson.' Both take directly opposed positions on whether truth-conveying is fiction's primary source of value.
explanations.A: Both accept this. Renata asserts it; Dmitri concedes it ('Fiction can certainly illuminate aspects of human experience'). Agreement in disguise.
explanations.B: Renata never denies that aesthetic properties have some value; she simply subordinates them to epistemic value. Dmitri affirms aesthetic value. Because Renata's position does not deny aesthetic value but only ranks it lower, both could accept that aesthetic properties have 'some' value — agreement in disguise, with a shift in subject from 'primary' to 'some.'
explanations.D: Renata explicitly argues for fiction's place in the curriculum; Dmitri never disputes this. One-sided trap — only one speaker addresses the curriculum question.
explanations.E: Renata asserts this; Dmitri does not address the comparative effectiveness of philosophical treatises. One-sided trap.
